text_blocks.snippet: Yes, COVID-19 has been associated with an increased risk of heart attacks. Studies have shown that individuals infected with COVID-19 may have a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, and premature death for years after the initial infection, even if they didn't experience severe illness. The risk may be even greater for those hospitalized with COVID-19, particularly in the early stages of the pandemic, according to www.heart.org. This increased risk appears to persist for up to three years after the initial infection. Additionally, there has been a rise in the number of heart attacks and strokes occurring in younger people, which has prompted research into the long-term cardiac effects of COVID-19.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, COVID-19 has been associated with an increased risk of heart attacks

text_blocks.snippet: The risk increase is not limited to severe cases. Studies from Mass General Brigham indicate that even mild or asymptomatic COVID-19 infections can contribute to a higher risk of future cardiac events. This suggests a broader impact of COVID-19 on cardiovascular health than previously understood.

text_blocks.snippet: COVID-19 can cause heart damage, including injury to the heart muscle (myocardial injury). Symptoms can include chest pain, shortness of breath, and swelling in the lower extremities. Some individuals with myocardial injury may not experience any symptoms. Diagnosing heart damage related to COVID-19 often involves blood tests and cardiac imaging according to the Cleveland Clinic.

Long-term changes: Research suggests that COVID-19 may lead to long-term changes in the heart, potentially increasing the risk of coronary artery disease, pulmonary hypertension, and valve problems.
